title: Trump Administration Reverses Disability Integration Rules
summary:
For nearly 50 years, the U.S. government has said people with disabilities should live, work, and learn in the most integrated setting possible — not be segregated in institutions like nursing homes. Last week, the Trump administration took its most concrete step yet to reverse that.

A federal judge agreed to strip mentions of 'integration' from federal regulations tied to Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, a landmark civil rights law. The judge did so after the Justice Department declined to defend its own rules in a lawsuit brought by several states.

Bruce Darling, president of the Center for Disability Rights, said hearing the ruling felt 'like a knife in your chest.' He said it suggests the government has decided disabled people 'don't have a right to live in freedom.'

Lawyer Jennifer Mathis said the decision did not undo protections under the Americans with Disabilities Act or the Supreme Court's Olmstead decision. But she worries about enforcement. The Justice Department did not respond to NPR's questions about why it changed course after decades of bipartisan support.
why_it_matters: Kids with disabilities go to school and take part in community life with everyone else partly because of these rules, so changing them can affect what schools, towns, and families can offer.

background_read: The Americans with Disabilities Act (a U.S. law passed in 1990) and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (a law from the 1970s) are two of the main laws that protect people with disabilities from being treated unfairly.
The Olmstead decision (a Supreme Court ruling) says people with disabilities have the right to live in their communities instead of being forced into institutions.
The Justice Department (the part of the U.S. government that enforces federal laws) usually defends the government's rules in court, so it is unusual for it to decline.
Article_Structure: WHO: A federal judge, the Justice Department, several states that sued, disability rights leader Bruce Darling of the Center for Disability Rights, and lawyer Jennifer Mathis.
WHAT: A judge agreed to strip mentions of 'integration' from federal regulations tied to Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, after the Justice Department declined to defend its own rules.
WHERE: In U.S. federal courts and federal regulations, which apply across the whole country.
WHY: For nearly 50 years the government said people with disabilities should live, work, and learn in the most integrated setting possible, and critics say this step moves away from that promise.

perspectives.description: Bruce Darling says the ruling felt 'like a knife in your chest' and suggests the government has decided disabled people 'don't have a right to live in freedom.'

The judge removed the word 'integration' from the rules only after the Justice Department refused to defend them in a lawsuit brought by several states; the department did not explain why it changed course.
Jennifer Mathis points out that the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Supreme Court's Olmstead decision were not undone, but she still worries that the rules will be harder to enforce.
